literature.title: The Earth is Flat because...: Investigating LLMs’ Belief towards Misinformation via Persuasive Conversation
literature.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) encapsulate vast amounts of knowledge but still remain vulnerable to external misinformation. Existing research mainly studied this susceptibility behavior in a single-turn setting. However, belief can change during a multi-turn conversation, especially a persuasive one. Therefore, in this study, we delve into LLMs’ susceptibility to persuasive conversations, particularly on factual questions that they can answer correctly. We first curate the Farm (i.e., Fact to Misinform) dataset, which contains factual questions paired with systematically generated persuasive misinformation. Then, we develop a testing framework to track LLMs’ belief changes in a persuasive dialogue. Through extensive experiments, we find that LLMs’ correct beliefs on factual knowledge can be easily manipulated by various persuasive strategies.

literature.title: End-to-end Learning of Logical Rules for Enhancing Document-level Relation Extraction
literature.abstract: Document-level relation extraction (DocRE) aims to extract relations between entities in a whole document. One of the pivotal challenges of DocRE is to capture the intricate interdependencies between relations of entity pairs. Previous methods have shown that logical rules can explicitly help capture such interdependencies. These methods either learn logical rules to refine the output of a trained DocRE model, or first learn logical rules from annotated data and then inject the learnt rules into a DocRE model using an auxiliary training objective. However, these learning pipelines may suffer from the issue of error propagation. To mitigate this issue, we propose Joint Modeling Relation extraction and Logical rules or JMRL for short, a novel rule-based framework that jointly learns both a DocRE model and logical rules in an end-to-end fashion. Specifically, we parameterize a rule reasoning module in JMRL to simulate the inference of logical rules, thereby explicitly modeling the reasoning process. We also introduce an auxiliary loss and a residual connection mechanism in JMRL to better reconcile the DocRE model and the rule reasoning module. Experimental results on four benchmark datasets demonstrate that our proposed JMRL framework is consistently superior to existing rule-based frameworks, improving five baseline models for DocRE by a significant margin.

literature.title: Confidence is not Timeless: Modeling Temporal Validity for Rule-based Temporal Knowledge Graph Forecasting
literature.abstract: Recently, Temporal Knowledge Graph Forecasting (TKGF) has emerged as a pivotal domain for forecasting future events. Unlike black-box neural network methods, rule-based approaches are lauded for their efficiency and interpretability. For this line of work, it is crucial to correctly estimate the predictive effectiveness of the rules, i.e., the confidence. However, the existing literature lacks in-depth investigation into how confidence evolves with time. Moreover, inaccurate and heuristic confidence estimation limits the performance of rule-based methods. To alleviate such issues, we propose a framework named TempValid to explicitly model the temporal validity of rules for TKGF. Specifically, we design a time function to model the interaction between temporal information with confidence. TempValid conceptualizes confidence and other coefficients as learnable parameters to avoid inaccurate estimation and combinatorial explosion. Furthermore, we introduce a rule-adversarial negative sampling and a time-aware negative sampling strategies to facilitate TempValid learning. Extensive experiments show that TempValid significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) rule-based methods on six TKGF datasets. Moreover, it exhibits substantial advancements in cross-domain and resource-constrained rule learning scenarios.

literature.title: Measuring and Benchmarking Large Language Models’ Capabilities to Generate Persuasive Language
literature.abstract: We are exposed to much information trying to influence us, such as teaser messages, debates, politically framed news, and propaganda — all of which use persuasive language. With the recent interest in Large Language Models (LLMs), we study the ability of LLMs to produce persuasive text. As opposed to prior work which focuses on particular domains or types of persuasion, we conduct a general study across various domains to measure and benchmark to what degree LLMs produce persuasive language - both when explicitly instructed to rewrite text to be more or less persuasive and when only instructed to paraphrase. We construct the new dataset Persuasive-Pairs of pairs of a short text and its rewrite by an LLM to amplify or diminish persuasive language. We multi-annotate the pairs on a relative scale for persuasive language: a valuable resource in itself, and for training a regression model to score and benchmark persuasive language, including for new LLMs across domains. In our analysis, we find that different ‘personas’ in LLaMA3’s system prompt change persuasive language substantially, even when only instructed to paraphrase.

literature.title: Can Language Models Serve as Text-Based World Simulators?
literature.abstract: Virtual environments play a key role in benchmarking advances in complex planning and decision-making tasks but are expensive and complicated to build by hand. Can current language models themselves serve as world simulators, correctly predicting how actions change different world states, thus bypassing the need for extensive manual coding? Our goal is to answer this question in the context of text-based simulators. Our approach is to build and use a new benchmark, called ByteSized32-State-Prediction, containing a dataset of text game state transitions and accompanying game tasks. We use this to directly quantify, for the first time, how well LLMs can serve as text-based world simulators. We test GPT-4 on this dataset and find that, despite its impressive performance, it is still an unreliable world simulator without further innovations. This work thus contributes both new insights into current LLM’s capabilities and weaknesses, as well as a novel benchmark to track future progress as new models appear.

literature.title: Can LLMs Reason with Rules? Logic Scaffolding for Stress-Testing and Improving LLMs
literature.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved impressive human-like performance across various reasoning tasks. However, their mastery of underlying inferential rules still falls short of human capabilities. To investigate this, we propose a logic scaffolding inferential rule generation framework, to construct an inferential rule base, ULogic, comprising both primitive and compositional rules across five domains. Our analysis of GPT-series models over a rule subset reveals significant gaps in LLMs’ logic understanding compared to human performance, especially in compositional and structural complex rules with certain bias patterns. We further distill these rules into a smaller-scale inference engine for flexible rule generation and enhancing downstream reasoning. Through a multi-judger evaluation, our inference engine proves effective in generating accurate, complex and abstract conclusions and premises, and improve various commonsense reasoning tasks. Overall, our work sheds light on LLMs’ limitations in grasping inferential rule and suggests ways to enhance their logical reasoning abilities .

literature.title: Rule or Story, Which is a Better Commonsense Expression for Talking with Large Language Models?
literature.abstract: Building machines with commonsense has been a longstanding challenge in NLP due to the reporting bias of commonsense rules and the exposure bias of rule-based commonsense reasoning. In contrast, humans convey and pass down commonsense implicitly through stories. This paper investigates the inherent commonsense ability of large language models (LLMs) expressed through storytelling. We systematically investigate and compare stories and rules for retrieving and leveraging commonsense in LLMs. Experimental results on 28 commonsense QA datasets show that stories outperform rules as the expression for retrieving commonsense from LLMs, exhibiting higher generation confidence and commonsense accuracy. Moreover, stories are the more effective commonsense expression for answering questions regarding daily events, while rules are more effective for scientific questions. This aligns with the reporting bias of commonsense in text corpora. We further show that the correctness and relevance of commonsense stories can be further improved via iterative self-supervised fine-tuning. These findings emphasize the importance of using appropriate language to express, retrieve, and leverage commonsense for LLMs, highlighting a promising direction for better exploiting their commonsense abilities.

initial_idea.title: Do Language-Model Explanations for Rule-Based Classification Track Underlying Rules or Maintain Persuasion under Minimal Counterfactual Rule Changes?
initial_idea.research_problem: Investigating whether post-hoc textual explanations generated by large language models for rule-based classification genuinely track the logical rules determining the prediction, or if they remain superficially persuasive and stable even when a minimal counterfactual modification to the underlying rule should logically reverse the classification outcome.
initial_idea.research_gap: While prior work explores multi-turn persuasion and belief manipulation in LLMs and evaluates logic scaffolding or rule-based reasoning, bounded search findings reveal an unexplored gap: there is no systematic evaluation of whether LLM-generated explanations for rule classifications faithfully track exact logical rule changes or exploit persuasive rhetoric to mask rule violations.
initial_idea.methodology: We construct a synthetic rule-following classification dataset with strict template-disjoint splits. Each sample pairs a deterministic multi-clause logical rule set, an instance, a ground-truth binary label, and an explanation. We apply minimal counterfactual rule changes (e.g., negating a critical clause) that mathematically flip the ground-truth label. We prompt candidate models to both classify the instance and generate a free-text explanation under the modified rules. We measure explanation fidelity by testing whether the generated text explicitly acknowledges the logical flip or persists with original justifications.
initial_idea.expected_contribution: We hypothesize that current LLM explanations are unfaithful to underlying rule changes, frequently retaining persuasive language that supports the original classification despite counterfactual logical modifications. We expect to demonstrate that explanation stability correlates with surface persuasiveness rather than logical faithfulness.
initial_idea.experimental_setup: We use Llama-3-8B-Instruct (resident weight memory ~16 GB under FP16, requiring CPU offload or execution on a 16GB+ target, or a smaller 3B model if restricted strictly to 12GB VRAM without offloading) accessed via HuggingFace transformers locally. The evaluation dataset comprises 1,000 seeded, synthetically generated logic-classification instances with paired counterfactual variants. We employ greedy decoding (temperature 0.0) for deterministic outputs and evaluate structural validity versus field-level semantic correctness using ground-truth label matching.
initial_idea.evaluation_strategy: We split the constructed dataset into 300 calibration instances (used for prompt tuning and validator calibration) and 700 held-out test instances. We aggregate exact confidence and binary classification metrics alongside semantic adherence scores. We use human-in-the-loop and rule-matching semantic adjudication on the test split, reporting exact match accuracy and counterfactual sensitivity scores with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals.
feasibility_assumptions: A 12GB consumer GPU can execute inference on a 3B parameter instruction-tuned model under 8-bit quantization or a 7B/8B model with CPU offload.
Template-disjoint data generation can cleanly separate logical rule variations without introducing structural leakage.
Automated regex and logical interpreters can reliably extract classification decisions and rule references from free-text model outputs.

final_idea.title: Do Language-Model Explanations for Rule-Based Classification Track Underlying Rules or Maintain Persuasion under Minimal Counterfactual Rule Changes?
final_idea.research_problem: Investigating whether post-hoc textual explanations generated by large language models for rule-based classification genuinely track the logical rules determining the prediction, or if they remain superficially stable due to token inertia or rhetorical persistence even when a minimal counterfactual modification to the underlying rule logically reverses the classification outcome.
final_idea.research_gap: While prior work explores multi-turn persuasion, logical reasoning scaffolding, and counterfactual input edits, bounded search findings reveal an unexplored gap: there is no systematic evaluation isolating whether LLM-generated explanations for rule classifications faithfully track exact logical rule-clause flips or exhibit persistence driven by token inertia rather than active rhetorical deception.
final_idea.methodology: We construct a synthetic rule-following classification dataset with strict template-disjoint splits via a seeded generator and deterministic Python validator oracle. Each sample pairs a deterministic multi-clause logical rule set, an instance, a ground-truth binary label, and an explanation. We apply minimal counterfactual rule changes (e.g., negating a critical clause) that mathematically flip the ground-truth label. We prompt candidate models to both classify the instance and generate a free-text explanation under the modified rules. To resolve parser noise and control for attention dilution, we implement structured JSON output constraints via constrained decoding and add a high-salience control condition where negated clauses are explicitly highlighted at the beginning of the prompt. We evaluate explanation faithfulness using regular expression parsing, semantic entailment checks via a smaller auxiliary NLI model, and a correlational counterfactual test (CCT) following Siegel et al. (2024), alongside a deterministic symbolic verification oracle replacing vulnerable auxiliary NLI entailment checks to isolate structural logic failures from parsing noise.
final_idea.expected_contribution: We hypothesize that current LLM explanations are unfaithful to underlying rule changes, frequently retaining language that supports the original classification despite counterfactual logical modifications. We expect to demonstrate whether explanation persistence correlates with token inertia or surface persuasiveness, while high-salience formatting helps distinguish oversight from structural reasoning limitations.
final_idea.experimental_setup: We use Llama-3-8B-Instruct configured with 4-bit quantization (via bitsandbytes) to maintain a resident weight memory footprint of approximately 4.5 GB (8 billion parameters at 0.5 bytes per parameter, well below the 12 GB VRAM limit of a single consumer GPU without KV cache overhead), avoiding full CPU offloading. The evaluation dataset comprises 1,000 seeded, synthetically generated logic-classification instances with paired counterfactual variants. We employ greedy decoding (temperature 0.0) for deterministic outputs and evaluate structural validity versus field-level semantic correctness using ground-truth label matching.
final_idea.evaluation_strategy: We split the constructed dataset into 300 calibration instances (used for prompt tuning and validator calibration) and 700 held-out test instances. We aggregate exact confidence and binary classification metrics alongside semantic adherence scores. We use automated semantic entailment and rule-matching semantic adjudication on the test split, reporting exact match accuracy and counterfactual sensitivity scores with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals.

input_idea.title: Do Language-Model Explanations for Rule-Based Classification Track Underlying Rules or Maintain Persuasion under Minimal Counterfactual Rule Changes?
input_idea.research_problem: Investigating whether post-hoc textual explanations generated by large language models for rule-based classification genuinely track the logical rules determining the prediction, or if they remain superficially persuasive and stable even when a minimal counterfactual modification to the underlying rule should logically reverse the classification outcome.
input_idea.research_gap: While prior work explores multi-turn persuasion and belief manipulation in LLMs and evaluates logic scaffolding or rule-based reasoning, bounded search findings reveal an unexplored gap: there is no systematic evaluation of whether LLM-generated explanations for rule classifications faithfully track exact logical rule changes or exploit persuasive rhetoric to mask rule violations.
input_idea.methodology: We construct a synthetic rule-following classification dataset with strict template-disjoint splits. Each sample pairs a deterministic multi-clause logical rule set, an instance, a ground-truth binary label, and an explanation. We apply minimal counterfactual rule changes (e.g., negating a critical clause) that mathematically flip the ground-truth label. We prompt candidate models to both classify the instance and generate a free-text explanation under the modified rules. We measure explanation fidelity by testing whether the generated text explicitly acknowledges the logical flip or persists with original justifications.
input_idea.expected_contribution: We hypothesize that current LLM explanations are unfaithful to underlying rule changes, frequently retaining persuasive language that supports the original classification despite counterfactual logical modifications. We expect to demonstrate that explanation stability correlates with surface persuasiveness rather than logical faithfulness.
input_idea.experimental_setup: We use Llama-3-8B-Instruct (resident weight memory ~16 GB under FP16, requiring CPU offload or execution on a 16GB+ target, or a smaller 3B model if restricted strictly to 12GB VRAM without offloading) accessed via HuggingFace transformers locally. The evaluation dataset comprises 1,000 seeded, synthetically generated logic-classification instances with paired counterfactual variants. We employ greedy decoding (temperature 0.0) for deterministic outputs and evaluate structural validity versus field-level semantic correctness using ground-truth label matching.
input_idea.evaluation_strategy: We split the constructed dataset into 300 calibration instances (used for prompt tuning and validator calibration) and 700 held-out test instances. We aggregate exact confidence and binary classification metrics alongside semantic adherence scores. We use human-in-the-loop and rule-matching semantic adjudication on the test split, reporting exact match accuracy and counterfactual sensitivity scores with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals.
feasibility_assumptions: A 12GB consumer GPU can execute inference on a 3B parameter instruction-tuned model under 8-bit quantization or a 7B/8B model with CPU offload.
Template-disjoint data generation can cleanly separate logical rule variations without introducing structural leakage.
Automated regex and logical interpreters can reliably extract classification decisions and rule references from free-text model outputs.

assumption_checks.assumption: The rule-generation pipeline produces unambiguous ground-truth labels that a symbolic solver can verify without ambiguity.
assumption_checks.validation_step: Run a symbolic Python interpreter over 50 randomly sampled generated rule sets and verify 100% agreement with template tags.
assumption_checks.acceptance_criterion: Zero logical contradictions or unresolvable clauses across the sample.
assumption_checks.fallback: Tighten template constraints and simplify rule clause depth.

assumption_checks.assumption: Model outputs can be reliably parsed for binary classifications and referenced rules using regular expressions.
assumption_checks.validation_step: Parse outputs from a 50-sample pilot run and manually inspect parsing failures.
assumption_checks.acceptance_criterion: Parsing success rate of at least 95%.
assumption_checks.fallback: Incorporate structured JSON output constraints via constrained decoding.

prior_work_comparison.proposed_difference: Extends static logic testing to evaluate post-hoc explanation faithfulness under minimal counterfactual rule modifications.
prior_work_comparison.verification_needed: Verify whether explanation persistence correlates with complex rule structures identified in prior work.

prior_work_comparison.shared_mechanism: Measures and benchmarks persuasive language generation capabilities across different model prompts and personas.

input_idea.core_hypothesis: Language model explanations for rule-based classification fail to track minimal counterfactual rule changes, maintaining high persuasive similarity to original justifications even when the underlying rule logically reverses the prediction.
input_idea.distinctive_mechanism: Coupling a controlled, template-disjoint counterfactual rule-flipping dataset with automated semantic rule-tracking checks to measure explanation unfaithfulness.
input_idea.minimum_test: Evaluate Llama-3-8B-Instruct on the test split of 700 counterfactual rule-flipping instances, measuring the rate at which generated explanations correctly cite the modified rule clause versus repeating original justifications.

review.explanation: The proposal aims to investigate whether LLM-generated explanations for rule-based classification remain superficially persuasive and stable under minimal counterfactual rule modifications rather than tracking the logical rule changes. While prior work evaluates counterfactual faithfulness or robustness of free-text explanations using input edits (such as Siegel et al., 2024), and others study logical rule scaffolding or counterfactual logical modifications in argumentative text (Huang et al., 2024), combining a template-disjoint synthetic rule-following dataset with automated counterfactual rule-flipping checks specifically to evaluate explanation unfaithfulness and persistence of persuasion presents an adequate level of novelty.
problems: The distinction between measuring standard explanation faithfulness via counterfactual input edits and testing rule-clause tracking under counterfactual rule changes needs sharper formalization.
Relying solely on automated regular expression parsing to interpret complex free-text model outputs and rule references may introduce significant noise.
improvements: Incorporate established metrics for evaluating explanation faithfulness such as the correlational counterfactual test (CCT) alongside the proposed rule-matching scores.
Expand validation steps for parser accuracy using secondary LLM-based verification or structured JSON decoding to ensure robust extraction of rule references.

evidence.claim: Prior work introduces counterfactual input edits to evaluate the faithfulness of free-text explanations.
evidence.supporting_excerpt: In this work, we introduce the correlational counterfactual test (CCT), a faithfulness metric based on counterfactual input edits that takes into account not just the binary label change, but the total shift in the model’s predicted label distribution.

evidence.claim: Prior research explores counterfactual reasoning capabilities and logical modifications in large language models.
evidence.supporting_excerpt: In this study, we delve into the realm of counterfactual reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs).

review.uncertainty: The novelty score is bounded by the existing literature on counterfactual evaluation of free-text explanations and logical rule reasoning tasks; however, the specific focus on persuasive persistence under minimal rule-clause flips provides moderate differentiation.
tradeoffs: Relying on synthetic rule datasets ensures clean ground-truth control but may limit the ecological validity of the findings compared to natural rule-based reasoning settings.
review.falsification_test: If empirical results show that Llama-3-8B-Instruct perfectly adapts its explanations and shifts its cited clauses on >95% of counterfactual rule flips, the core hypothesis that explanations maintain unfaithful persuasive stability would be falsified.

papers.title: On Measuring Faithfulness or Self-consistency of Natural Language Explanations
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can explain their predictions through post-hoc or Chain-of-Thought (CoT) explanations. But an LLM could make up reasonably sounding explanations that are unfaithful to its underlying reasoning. Recent work has designed tests that aim to judge the faithfulness of post-hoc or CoT explanations. In this work we argue that these faithfulness tests do not measure faithfulness to the models’ inner workings – but rather their self-consistency at output level.Our contributions are three-fold: i) We clarify the status of faithfulness tests in view of model explainability, characterising them as self-consistency tests instead. This assessment we underline by ii) constructing a Comparative Consistency Bank for self-consistency tests that for the first time compares existing tests on a common suite of 11 open LLMs and 5 tasks – including iii) our new self-consistency measure CC-SHAP. CC-SHAP is a fine-grained measure (not a test) of LLM self-consistency. It compares how a model’s input contributes to the predicted answer and to generating the explanation. Our fine-grained CC-SHAP metric allows us iii) to compare LLM behaviour when making predictions and to analyse the effect of other consistency tests at a deeper level, which takes us one step further towards measuring faithfulness by bringing us closer to the internals of the model than strictly surface output-oriented tests.

papers.title: The Probabilities Also Matter: A More Faithful Metric for Faithfulness of Free-Text Explanations in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: In order to oversee advanced AI systems, it is important to understand their reasons for generating a given output. When prompted, large language models (LLMs) can provide natural language explanations or reasoning traces that sound plausible and receive high ratings from human annotators. However, it is unclear to what extent these explanations are truly capturing the factors responsible for the model’s predictions: the most “human-like” explanation may be different from the one that is most faithful to the model’s true decision making process. In this work, we introduce the correlational counterfactual test (CCT), a faithfulness metric based on counterfactual input edits that takes into account not just the binary label change, but the total shift in the model’s predicted label distribution. We evaluate the faithfulness of free-text explanations generated by few-shot-prompted LLMs from the Llama-2 family on three NLP tasks. We find that these explanations are indeed more likely to mention factors when they are impactful to the model’s prediction, with the degree of association increasing with model size but varying significantly by task.

papers.title: Main Predicate and Their Arguments as Explanation Signals For Intent Classification
papers.abstract: Intent classification is crucial for conversational agents (chatbots), and deep learning models perform well in this area. However, little research has been done on the explainability of intent classification due to the absence of suitable benchmark data. Human annotation of explanation signals in text samples is time-consuming and costly. However, from inspection of data on intent classification, we see that, more often than not, the main verb denotes the action, and the direct object indicates the domain of conversation, serving as explanation signals for intent. This observation enables us to hypothesize that the main predicate in the text utterances, along with the arguments of the main predicate, can serve as explanation signals. Leveraging this, we introduce a new technique to automatically augment text samples from intent classification datasets with word-level explanations. We mark main predicates (primarily verbs) and their arguments (dependency relations) as explanation signals in benchmark intent classification datasets ATIS and SNIPS, creating a unique 21k-instance dataset for explainability. Further, we experiment with deep learning and language models. We observe that models that work well for classification do not perform well in explainability metrics like plausibility and faithfulness. We also observe that guiding models to focus on explanation signals from our dataset during training improves the plausibility Token F1 score by 3-4%, improving the model’s reasoning.

papers.title: Reasoning Aware Self-Consistency: Leveraging Reasoning Paths for Efficient LLM Sampling
papers.abstract: Self-consistency mitigates hallucinations in Large Language Models (LLMs) by sampling multiple reasoning paths, but it lacks a systematic approach to determine the optimal number of samples or select the most faithful rationale. To address this limitation, we introduce Reasoning-Aware Self-Consistency (RASC), a novel framework that enhances sampling efficiency and reasoning faithfulness by dynamically evaluating both outputs and rationales. RASC assesses the quality of reasoning and the consistency of answers for each generated sample, using these assessments to guide early stopping decisions and rationale selection. The framework employs criteria-based stopping and weighted majority voting, enabling more informed choices on when to halt sampling and which rationale to select. Our comprehensive experiments across diverse question-answering datasets demonstrate that RASC outperforms existing methods, reducing sample usage by approximately 70% while maintaining accuracy. Moreover, RASC facilitates the selection of high-fidelity rationales, thereby improving the faithfulness of LLM outputs. Our approach effectively addresses the efficiency-accuracy trade-off in LLM reasoning tasks, offering a new perspective for more nuanced, faithful, and effective utilization of LLMs in resource-constrained environments.

papers.title: One Prompt To Rule Them All: LLMs for Opinion Summary Evaluation
papers.abstract: Evaluation of opinion summaries using conventional reference-based metrics often fails to provide a comprehensive assessment and exhibits limited correlation with human judgments. While Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promise as reference-free metrics for NLG evaluation, their potential remains unexplored for opinion summary evaluation. Furthermore, the absence of sufficient opinion summary evaluation datasets hinders progress in this area. In response, we introduce the SUMMEVAL-OP dataset, encompassing 7 dimensions crucial to the evaluation of opinion summaries: fluency, coherence, relevance, faithfulness, aspect coverage, sentiment consistency, and specificity. We propose OP-I-PROMPT, a dimension-independent prompt, along with OP-PROMPTS, a dimension-dependent set of prompts for opinion summary evaluation. Our experiments demonstrate that OP-I-PROMPT emerges as a good alternative for evaluating opinion summaries, achieving an average Spearman correlation of 0.70 with human judgments, surpassing prior methodologies. Remarkably, we are the first to explore the efficacy of LLMs as evaluators, both on closed-source and open-source models, in the opinion summary evaluation domain.

papers.title: From Generating Answers to Building Explanations: Integrating Multi-Round RAG and Causal Modeling for Scientific QA
papers.abstract: Application of LLMs for complex causal question answering can be stymied by their opacity and propensity for hallucination. Although recent approaches such as Retrieval Augmented Generation and Chain of Thought prompting have improved reliability, we argue current approaches are insufficient and further fail to satisfy key criteria humans use to select and evaluate causal explanations. Inspired by findings from the social sciences, we present an implemented causal QA approach that combines iterative RAG with guidance from a formal model of causation. Our causal model is backed by the Cogent reasoning engine, allowing users to interactively perform counterfactual analysis and refine their answer. Our approach has been integrated into a deployed Collaborative Research Assistant (Cora) and we present a pilot evaluation in the life sciences domain.

papers.title: CLOMO: Counterfactual Logical Modification with Large Language Models
papers.abstract: In this study, we delve into the realm of counterfactual reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). Our primary objective is to cultivate the counterfactual thought processes within LLMs and rigorously assess these processes for their validity. Specifically, we introduce a novel task, Counterfactual Logical Modification (CLOMO), and a high-quality human-annotated benchmark. In this task, LLMs must adeptly alter a given argumentative text to uphold a predetermined logical relationship. To effectively evaluate a generation model’s counterfactual capabilities, we propose an innovative evaluation metric, the decomposed Self-Evaluation Score (SES) to directly evaluate the natural language output of LLMs instead of modeling the task as a multiple-choice problem. Analysis shows that the proposed automatic metric aligns well with human preference. Our experimental results show that while LLMs demonstrate a notable capacity for logical counterfactual thinking, there remains a discernible gap between their current abilities and human performance. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Eleanor-H/CLOMO.

papers.title: Multi-Aspect Controllable Text Generation with Disentangled Counterfactual Augmentation
papers.abstract: Multi-aspect controllable text generation aims to control the generated texts in attributes from multiple aspects (e.g., “positive” from sentiment and “sport” from topic). Existing works neglect attribute correlations formed by the intertwining of different attributes. Particularly, the stereotype formed by imbalanced attribute correlations significantly affects multi-aspect control. In this paper, we propose MAGIC, a new multi-aspect controllable text generation method with disentangled counterfactual augmentation. We alleviate the issue of imbalanced attribute correlations during training using counterfactual feature vectors in the attribute latent space by disentanglement. During inference, we enhance attribute correlations by target-guided counterfactual augmentation to further improve multi-aspect control. Experiments show that MAGIC outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both imbalanced and balanced attribute correlation scenarios.

papers.title: Born Differently Makes a Difference: Counterfactual Study of Bias in Biography Generation from a Data-to-Text Perspective
papers.abstract: How do personal attributes affect biography generation? Addressing this question requires an identical pair of biographies where only the personal attributes of interest are different. However, it is rare in the real world. To address this, we propose a counterfactual methodology from a data-to-text perspective, manipulating the personal attributes of interest while keeping the co-occurring attributes unchanged. We first validate that the fine-tuned Flan-T5 model generates the biographies based on the given attributes. This work expands the analysis of gender-centered bias in text generation. Our results confirm the well-known bias in gender and also show the bias in regions, in both individual and its related co-occurring attributes in semantic machining and sentiment.

papers.title: Measuring and Benchmarking Large Language Models’ Capabilities to Generate Persuasive Language
papers.abstract: We are exposed to much information trying to influence us, such as teaser messages, debates, politically framed news, and propaganda — all of which use persuasive language. With the recent interest in Large Language Models (LLMs), we study the ability of LLMs to produce persuasive text. As opposed to prior work which focuses on particular domains or types of persuasion, we conduct a general study across various domains to measure and benchmark to what degree LLMs produce persuasive language - both when explicitly instructed to rewrite text to be more or less persuasive and when only instructed to paraphrase. We construct the new dataset Persuasive-Pairs of pairs of a short text and its rewrite by an LLM to amplify or diminish persuasive language. We multi-annotate the pairs on a relative scale for persuasive language: a valuable resource in itself, and for training a regression model to score and benchmark persuasive language, including for new LLMs across domains. In our analysis, we find that different ‘personas’ in LLaMA3’s system prompt change persuasive language substantially, even when only instructed to paraphrase.

papers.title: Evaluating Intention Detection Capability of Large Language Models in Persuasive Dialogues
papers.abstract: We investigate intention detection in persuasive multi-turn dialogs employing the largest available Large Language Models (LLMs).Much of the prior research measures the intention detection capability of machine learning models without considering the conversational history.To evaluate LLMs’ intention detection capability in conversation, we modified the existing datasets of persuasive conversation and created datasets using a multiple-choice paradigm.It is crucial to consider others’ perspectives through their utterances when engaging in a persuasive conversation, especially when making a request or reply that is inconvenient for others.This feature makes the persuasive dialogue suitable for the dataset of measuring intention detection capability.We incorporate the concept of ‘face acts,’ which categorize how utterances affect mental states.This approach enables us to measure intention detection capability by focusing on crucial intentions and to conduct comprehensible analysis according to intention types.

papers.title: The Earth is Flat because...: Investigating LLMs’ Belief towards Misinformation via Persuasive Conversation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) encapsulate vast amounts of knowledge but still remain vulnerable to external misinformation. Existing research mainly studied this susceptibility behavior in a single-turn setting. However, belief can change during a multi-turn conversation, especially a persuasive one. Therefore, in this study, we delve into LLMs’ susceptibility to persuasive conversations, particularly on factual questions that they can answer correctly. We first curate the Farm (i.e., Fact to Misinform) dataset, which contains factual questions paired with systematically generated persuasive misinformation. Then, we develop a testing framework to track LLMs’ belief changes in a persuasive dialogue. Through extensive experiments, we find that LLMs’ correct beliefs on factual knowledge can be easily manipulated by various persuasive strategies.

papers.title: Logic-of-Thought: Injecting Logic into Contexts for Full Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across various tasks but their performance in complex logical reasoning tasks remains unsatisfactory. Although some prompting methods, such as Chain-of-Thought, can improve the reasoning ability of LLMs to some extent, they suffer from an unfaithful issue where derived conclusions may not align with the generated reasoning chain. To address this issue, some studies employ the approach of propositional logic to further enhance logical reasoning abilities of LLMs. However, the potential omissions in the extraction of logical expressions in these methods can cause information loss in the logical reasoning process, thereby generating incorrect results. To this end, we propose Logic-of-Thought (LoT) prompting which employs propositional logic to generate expanded logical information descriptions and utilizes them as an additional augmentation to original contexts, thereby ensuring information completeness and enhancing logical reasoning ability. LoT is orthogonal to existing prompting methods and can be seamlessly integrated with them. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LoT boosts the performance of various prompting methods with a striking margin across five logical reasoning tasks. In particular, LoT enhances Chain-of-Thought’s performance on the ReClor dataset by +4.35%, improves Chain-of-Thought with Self-Consistency’s performance on the RuleTaker dataset by +3.52%, and boosts performance of Tree-of-Thoughts on the ProofWriter dataset by +8%.

papers.title: Communication Makes Perfect: Persuasion Dataset Construction via Multi-LLM Communication
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown proficiency in generating persuasive dialogue, yet concerns about the fluency and sophistication of their outputs persist. This paper presents a multi-LLM communication framework designed to enhance the generation of persuasive data automatically. This framework facilitates the efficient production of high-quality, diverse linguistic content with minimal human oversight. Through extensive evaluations, we demonstrate that the generated data excels in naturalness, linguistic diversity, and the strategic use of persuasion, even in complex scenarios involving social taboos. The framework also proves adept at generalizing across novel contexts. Our results highlight the framework’s potential to significantly advance research in both computational and social science domains concerning persuasive communication.

review.explanation: The proposal presents a well-structured empirical study investigating whether LLM-generated explanations for rule-based classifications faithfully track minimal counterfactual rule changes. The methodology leverages a synthetic rule dataset and checks explanation stability versus semantic logic changes. However, the experimental setup claims that LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct (approx. 16GB in FP16) can run on a 12GB consumer GPU via CPU offload or execution on a 16GB+ target, while also mentioning a 3B model as an alternative. Since the project constraints explicitly limit resources to 1 single consumer GPU (12GB) with no LLM training, running an 8B model locally requires 8-bit or 4-bit quantization (e.g., via bitsandbytes or GPTQ/AWQ) rather than raw FP16 or full CPU offloading to maintain reasonable inference speed. The validation plan handles regular expression parsing risks, but requires a formal pilot memory test under quantization to confirm local feasibility on the 12GB device.
problems: The hardware assumption states that LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct requires FP16 residency of ~16 GB, which exceeds the 12GB consumer GPU limit without explicit quantization strategies.
Relying solely on regular expressions to parse free-text explanations and complex rule references can be fragile and introduce noise into counterfactual sensitivity scores.
improvements: Specify explicit 4-bit or 8-bit quantization (e.g., using bitsandbytes or HuggingFace transformers with BitsAndBytesConfig) for LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct to ensure memory footprint remains safely under the 12GB VRAM limit during inference.
Adopt structured decoding constraints (such as Outlines or JSON schema-guided generation) alongside regular expressions to ensure model outputs adhere to a parseable format.

review.uncertainty: It remains uncertain whether regular expression parsing can reliably extract counterfactual rule clauses from free-text explanations without manual annotation verification or constrained decoding.
tradeoffs: Using a larger 8B model provides better instruction-following fidelity at the cost of requiring aggressive 4-bit/8-bit quantization to fit within 12GB VRAM constraints.
review.falsification_test: If a pilot test on 50 instances shows that 4-bit quantized LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct fails to maintain a parseable output success rate of at least 95% using regex and structural checks, the evaluation must fall back to a smaller 3B instruction-tuned model or incorporate constrained decoding.

review.explanation: The proposal clearly defines an experimental protocol to test whether LLM-generated explanations for rule classifications track logical rule updates or retain persuasive justifications. The methodology uses template-disjoint synthetic rule sets and minimal counterfactual modifications to isolate explanation unfaithfulness. However, the proposal would benefit from more precise operational definitions of persuasive language versus logical faithfulness.
problems: The operational distinction between surface persuasiveness and logical faithfulness lacks a quantitative metric in the core description.
Relying entirely on regular expressions to parse free-text explanations for rule references may introduce parser noise when models vary their phrasing style.
improvements: Incorporate a validated textual persuasion score (such as regression models trained on persuasive pairs) to explicitly measure the persistence of rhetorical style.
Provide clearer formal criteria or scoring rubrics for human-in-the-loop and rule-matching semantic adjudication.

evidence.claim: Systematic evaluation of language model behavior using curated benchmarks provides crucial insights into model limitations and weaknesses.
evidence.supporting_excerpt: This work thus contributes both new insights into current LLM’s capabilities and weaknesses, as well as a novel benchmark to track future progress as new models appear.

review.uncertainty: The proposal remains uncertain about how robust regex and rule interpreters will be against creative paraphrasing in free-text model explanations.
tradeoffs: Using a smaller 3B model or 8-bit quantization to fit within a 12GB VRAM constraint may reduce instruction-following fidelity compared to larger base models.
review.falsification_test: If models exhibit near-100% sensitivity to counterfactual rule changes by instantly adapting their explanations to cite modified clauses without residual persuasive persistence, the core hypothesis that explanations mask rule violations via rhetoric would be falsified.

review.explanation: The central premise assumes that language model explanations are autonomous entities operating independently of classification logic, where persistence of text stems from persuasion rather than simpler alternatives like prompt-template inertia, next-token continuation artifacts, or the strong prior distribution of the target instance text overriding subtle rule negation clauses. Furthermore, testing a single model (Llama-3-8B-Instruct) under zero-shot or few-shot prompts risks conflating instruction-following failures with unfaithfulness or persuasive masking.
problems: The evaluation fails to distinguish between genuine persuasive masking and a simpler failure mode: language models frequently suffer from attention dilution and fail to notice small textual edits (like a single negation) in long rule descriptions, treating the counterfactual rule as identical to the training distribution.

The methodology relies on regular expressions and symbolic interpreters to check whether generated text explicitly acknowledges logical flips; however, text generation models often produce valid reasoning through paraphrases that bypass rigid regex patterns, leading to false positives for unfaithfulness.

The scope is restricted to a single model (Llama-3-8B-Instruct), which limits generalizability and leaves open the possibility that the observed unfaithfulness is merely a side-effect of quantization or prompt sensitivity rather than a fundamental property of LLM explanations.
improvements: Introduce a control condition where rule modifications are made glaringly obvious via formatting highlights or explicit prompt cues to determine whether unfaithfulness stems from oversight or active persuasion.
Replace fragile regular expression checks with semantic entailment verification using an independent entailment model to assess whether the explanation logically supports the new label.
Expand the model evaluation suite to include multiple model scales and instruction-tuning variants to verify if explanation fidelity scales with parameter count.

evidence.claim: Large language models exhibit impressive performance across tasks but struggle with strict rule mastery.
evidence.supporting_excerpt: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved impressive human-like performance across various reasoning tasks.

evidence.claim: Mastery of underlying inferential rules in LLMs falls short of human capabilities.
evidence.supporting_excerpt: However, their mastery of underlying inferential rules still falls short of human capabilities.

review.uncertainty: The primary limitation is that text generation patterns are heavily confounded by surface-level prompt formatting and token priors, making it difficult to isolate active persuasion from simple reading comprehension failures without additional probing controls.
tradeoffs: Using synthetic rules guarantees ground truth and clean counterfactuals, but limits ecological validity compared to real-world policy documents or legal statutes.
review.falsification_test: To distinguish active persuasion from simple oversight (failure to notice the rule change), test the model using a condition where the negated clause is placed in the primary focus position (e.g., the very first sentence) and explicitly highlighted with visual markers. If explanation unfaithfulness drops to zero under high-salience conditions, the failure is driven by attention limits and input oversight rather than an inherent drive to maintain persuasion.

Since the project constraints explicitly limit resources to 1 single consumer GPU (12GB) with no LLM training, running an 8B model locally requires 8-bit or 4-bit quantization (e.g., via bitsandbytes or GPTQ/AWQ) rather than raw FP16 or full CPU offloading to maintain reasonable inference speed. The validation plan handles regular expression parsing risks, but requires a formal pilot memory test under quantization to confirm local feasibility on the 12GB device.
problems: The hardware assumption states that LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct requires FP16 residency of ~16 GB, which exceeds the 12GB consumer GPU limit without explicit quantization strategies.
Relying solely on regular expressions to parse free-text explanations and complex rule references can be fragile and introduce noise into counterfactual sensitivity scores.
improvements: Specify explicit 4-bit or 8-bit quantization (e.g., using bitsandbytes or HuggingFace transformers with BitsAndBytesConfig) for LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct to ensure memory footprint remains safely under the 12GB VRAM limit during inference.
Adopt structured decoding constraints (such as Outlines or JSON schema-guided generation) alongside regular expressions to ensure model outputs adhere to a parseable format.

evidence.claim: LLMs can be studied across various domains to measure the degree to which they produce persuasive language.
evidence.supporting_excerpt: As opposed to prior work which focuses on particular domains or types of persuasion, we conduct a general study across various domains to measure and benchmark to what degree LLMs produce persuasive language - both when explicitly instructed to rewrite text to be more or less persuasive and when only instructed to paraphrase.

independent_reviews.uncertainty: It remains uncertain whether regular expression parsing can reliably extract counterfactual rule clauses from free-text explanations without manual annotation verification or constrained decoding.
tradeoffs: Using a larger 8B model provides better instruction-following fidelity at the cost of requiring aggressive 4-bit/8-bit quantization to fit within 12GB VRAM constraints.
independent_reviews.falsification_test: If a pilot test on 50 instances shows that 4-bit quantized LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct fails to maintain a parseable output success rate of at least 95% using regex and structural checks, the evaluation must fall back to a smaller 3B instruction-tuned model or incorporate constrained decoding.

independent_reviews.explanation: The proposal clearly defines an experimental protocol to test whether LLM-generated explanations for rule classifications track logical rule updates or retain persuasive justifications. The methodology uses template-disjoint synthetic rule sets and minimal counterfactual modifications to isolate explanation unfaithfulness. However, the proposal would benefit from more precise operational definitions of persuasive language versus logical faithfulness.
problems: The operational distinction between surface persuasiveness and logical faithfulness lacks a quantitative metric in the core description.
Relying entirely on regular expressions to parse free-text explanations for rule references may introduce parser noise when models vary their phrasing style.
improvements: Incorporate a validated textual persuasion score (such as regression models trained on persuasive pairs) to explicitly measure the persistence of rhetorical style.
Provide clearer formal criteria or scoring rubrics for human-in-the-loop and rule-matching semantic adjudication.

evidence.claim: Systematic evaluation of language model behavior using curated benchmarks provides crucial insights into model limitations and weaknesses.
evidence.supporting_excerpt: This work thus contributes both new insights into current LLM’s capabilities and weaknesses, as well as a novel benchmark to track future progress as new models appear.

independent_reviews.uncertainty: The proposal remains uncertain about how robust regex and rule interpreters will be against creative paraphrasing in free-text model explanations.
tradeoffs: Using a smaller 3B model or 8-bit quantization to fit within a 12GB VRAM constraint may reduce instruction-following fidelity compared to larger base models.
independent_reviews.falsification_test: If models exhibit near-100% sensitivity to counterfactual rule changes by instantly adapting their explanations to cite modified clauses without residual persuasive persistence, the core hypothesis that explanations mask rule violations via rhetoric would be falsified.

independent_reviews.explanation: The central premise assumes that language model explanations are autonomous entities operating independently of classification logic, where persistence of text stems from persuasion rather than simpler alternatives like prompt-template inertia, next-token continuation artifacts, or the strong prior distribution of the target instance text overriding subtle rule negation clauses. Furthermore, testing a single model (Llama-3-8B-Instruct) under zero-shot or few-shot prompts risks conflating instruction-following failures with unfaithfulness or persuasive masking.
problems: The evaluation fails to distinguish between genuine persuasive masking and a simpler failure mode: language models frequently suffer from attention dilution and fail to notice small textual edits (like a single negation) in long rule descriptions, treating the counterfactual rule as identical to the training distribution.

The methodology relies on regular expressions and symbolic interpreters to check whether generated text explicitly acknowledges logical flips; however, text generation models often produce valid reasoning through paraphrases that bypass rigid regex patterns, leading to false positives for unfaithfulness.

The scope is restricted to a single model (Llama-3-8B-Instruct), which limits generalizability and leaves open the possibility that the observed unfaithfulness is merely a side-effect of quantization or prompt sensitivity rather than a fundamental property of LLM explanations.
improvements: Introduce a control condition where rule modifications are made glaringly obvious via formatting highlights or explicit prompt cues to determine whether unfaithfulness stems from oversight or active persuasion.
Replace fragile regular expression checks with semantic entailment verification using an independent entailment model to assess whether the explanation logically supports the new label.
Expand the model evaluation suite to include multiple model scales and instruction-tuning variants to verify if explanation fidelity scales with parameter count.

If explanation unfaithfulness drops to zero under high-salience conditions, the failure is driven by attention limits and input oversight rather than an inherent drive to maintain persuasion.

revised_idea.title: Do Language-Model Explanations for Rule-Based Classification Track Underlying Rules or Maintain Persuasion under Minimal Counterfactual Rule Changes?
revised_idea.research_problem: Investigating whether post-hoc textual explanations generated by large language models for rule-based classification genuinely track the logical rules determining the prediction, or if they remain superficially persuasive and stable even when a minimal counterfactual modification to the underlying rule should logically reverse the classification outcome.
revised_idea.research_gap: While prior work explores multi-turn persuasion, logical reasoning scaffolding, and counterfactual input edits, bounded search findings reveal an unexplored gap: there is no systematic evaluation isolating whether LLM-generated explanations for rule classifications faithfully track exact logical rule-clause flips or exploit persuasive rhetoric to mask rule violations.
revised_idea.methodology: We construct a synthetic rule-following classification dataset with strict template-disjoint splits. Each sample pairs a deterministic multi-clause logical rule set, an instance, a ground-truth binary label, and an explanation. We apply minimal counterfactual rule changes (e.g., negating a critical clause) that mathematically flip the ground-truth label. We prompt candidate models to both classify the instance and generate a free-text explanation under the modified rules. To resolve parser noise and control for attention dilution, we implement structured JSON output constraints via constrained decoding and add a high-salience control condition where negated clauses are explicitly highlighted at the beginning of the prompt. We evaluate explanation faithfulness using both regular expression parsing for explicit rule references and a correlational counterfactual test (CCT) following Siegel et al. (2024).
revised_idea.expected_contribution: We hypothesize that current LLM explanations are unfaithful to underlying rule changes, frequently retaining persuasive language that supports the original classification despite counterfactual logical modifications. We expect to demonstrate that explanation stability correlates with surface persuasiveness rather than logical faithfulness, while high-salience formatting helps distinguish oversight from active rhetorical masking.
revised_idea.experimental_setup: We use Llama-3-8B-Instruct configured with 4-bit quantization (via bitsandbytes) to maintain a resident weight memory footprint well below the 12 GB VRAM limit of a single consumer GPU, avoiding full CPU offloading. The evaluation dataset comprises 1,000 seeded, synthetically generated logic-classification instances with paired counterfactual variants. We employ greedy decoding (temperature 0.0) for deterministic outputs and evaluate structural validity versus field-level semantic correctness using ground-truth label matching.
revised_idea.evaluation_strategy: We split the constructed dataset into 300 calibration instances (used for prompt tuning and validator calibration) and 700 held-out test instances. We aggregate exact confidence and binary classification metrics alongside semantic adherence scores. We use human-in-the-loop and rule-matching semantic adjudication on the test split, reporting exact match accuracy and counterfactual sensitivity scores with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals.
feasibility_assumptions: A 12GB consumer GPU can execute inference on an 8-parameter instruction-tuned model under 4-bit quantization (bitsandbytes) while keeping peak VRAM under 10 GB.
Template-disjoint data generation can cleanly separate logical rule variations without introducing structural leakage.
Constrained decoding frameworks can reliably enforce structured JSON outputs to extract classification decisions and rule references without parser noise.

assumption_checks.assumption: The rule-generation pipeline produces unambiguous ground-truth labels that a symbolic solver can verify without ambiguity.
assumption_checks.validation_step: Run a symbolic Python interpreter over 50 randomly sampled generated rule sets and verify 100% agreement with template tags.
assumption_checks.acceptance_criterion: Zero logical contradictions or unresolvable clauses across the sample.
assumption_checks.fallback: Tighten template constraints and simplify rule clause depth.

assumption_checks.assumption: 4-bit quantization of Llama-3-8B-Instruct fits comfortably within 12GB VRAM and maintains parseable output success rates.
assumption_checks.validation_step: Execute a 50-sample pilot run using bitsandbytes 4-bit quantization, logging peak VRAM usage and JSON parsing success.
assumption_checks.acceptance_criterion: Peak VRAM stays below 11 GB and output parsing success is at least 95%.
assumption_checks.fallback: Fall back to a smaller 3B instruction-tuned model (e.g., Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct) under FP16 precision.

prior_work_comparison.shared_mechanism: Utilizes logical rule scaffolding and rule generation templates to test language model reasoning limits.
prior_work_comparison.proposed_difference: Extends static logic testing to evaluate post-hoc explanation faithfulness under minimal counterfactual rule modifications rather than static evaluation.
prior_work_comparison.verification_needed: Verify whether explanation persistence correlates with complex rule structures identified in prior work.

prior_work_comparison.shared_mechanism: Evaluates explanation faithfulness via counterfactual edits measuring probability shifts and label consistency.
prior_work_comparison.proposed_difference: Focuses on explicit counterfactual rule-clause flips and rhetorical persuasion persistence rather than continuous input feature masking.
prior_work_comparison.verification_needed: Confirm whether correlational counterfactual test metrics align with rule-clause tracking failures.

prior_work_comparison.shared_mechanism: Measures and benchmarks persuasive language generation capabilities across different model prompts and personas.
prior_work_comparison.proposed_difference: Isolates persuasive rhetoric in explanations to test if high persuasiveness masks underlying logical rule violations.
prior_work_comparison.verification_needed: Confirm whether persuasive phrasing scores predict failure to adapt explanations to counterfactual rule changes.

revised_idea.core_hypothesis: Language model explanations for rule-based classification fail to track minimal counterfactual rule changes, maintaining high persuasive similarity to original justifications even when the underlying rule logically reverses the prediction.
revised_idea.distinctive_mechanism: Coupling a controlled, template-disjoint counterfactual rule-flipping dataset with constrained decoding and automated semantic rule-tracking checks to measure explanation unfaithfulness.
revised_idea.minimum_test: Evaluate 4-bit quantized Llama-3-8B-Instruct on the test split of 700 counterfactual rule-flipping instances, measuring the rate at which generated explanations correctly cite the modified rule clause versus repeating original justifications under standard and high-salience prompt conditions.

input_verification.limitations: Bounded source coverage; LLM verdicts require human validation. Exact excerpts verify provenance, not semantic truth.
