literature.title: Confidence is not Timeless: Modeling Temporal Validity for Rule-based Temporal Knowledge Graph Forecasting
literature.abstract: Recently, Temporal Knowledge Graph Forecasting (TKGF) has emerged as a pivotal domain for forecasting future events. Unlike black-box neural network methods, rule-based approaches are lauded for their efficiency and interpretability. For this line of work, it is crucial to correctly estimate the predictive effectiveness of the rules, i.e., the confidence. However, the existing literature lacks in-depth investigation into how confidence evolves with time. Moreover, inaccurate and heuristic confidence estimation limits the performance of rule-based methods. To alleviate such issues, we propose a framework named TempValid to explicitly model the temporal validity of rules for TKGF. Specifically, we design a time function to model the interaction between temporal information with confidence. TempValid conceptualizes confidence and other coefficients as learnable parameters to avoid inaccurate estimation and combinatorial explosion. Furthermore, we introduce a rule-adversarial negative sampling and a time-aware negative sampling strategies to facilitate TempValid learning. Extensive experiments show that TempValid significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) rule-based methods on six TKGF datasets. Moreover, it exhibits substantial advancements in cross-domain and resource-constrained rule learning scenarios.

literature.title: Measuring and Benchmarking Large Language Models’ Capabilities to Generate Persuasive Language
literature.abstract: We are exposed to much information trying to influence us, such as teaser messages, debates, politically framed news, and propaganda — all of which use persuasive language. With the recent interest in Large Language Models (LLMs), we study the ability of LLMs to produce persuasive text. As opposed to prior work which focuses on particular domains or types of persuasion, we conduct a general study across various domains to measure and benchmark to what degree LLMs produce persuasive language - both when explicitly instructed to rewrite text to be more or less persuasive and when only instructed to paraphrase. We construct the new dataset Persuasive-Pairs of pairs of a short text and its rewrite by an LLM to amplify or diminish persuasive language. We multi-annotate the pairs on a relative scale for persuasive language: a valuable resource in itself, and for training a regression model to score and benchmark persuasive language, including for new LLMs across domains. In our analysis, we find that different ‘personas’ in LLaMA3’s system prompt change persuasive language substantially, even when only instructed to paraphrase.

literature.title: Can Language Models Serve as Text-Based World Simulators?
literature.abstract: Virtual environments play a key role in benchmarking advances in complex planning and decision-making tasks but are expensive and complicated to build by hand. Can current language models themselves serve as world simulators, correctly predicting how actions change different world states, thus bypassing the need for extensive manual coding? Our goal is to answer this question in the context of text-based simulators. Our approach is to build and use a new benchmark, called ByteSized32-State-Prediction, containing a dataset of text game state transitions and accompanying game tasks. We use this to directly quantify, for the first time, how well LLMs can serve as text-based world simulators. We test GPT-4 on this dataset and find that, despite its impressive performance, it is still an unreliable world simulator without further innovations. This work thus contributes both new insights into current LLM’s capabilities and weaknesses, as well as a novel benchmark to track future progress as new models appear.

literature.title: Can LLMs Reason with Rules? Logic Scaffolding for Stress-Testing and Improving LLMs
literature.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved impressive human-like performance across various reasoning tasks. However, their mastery of underlying inferential rules still falls short of human capabilities. To investigate this, we propose a logic scaffolding inferential rule generation framework, to construct an inferential rule base, ULogic, comprising both primitive and compositional rules across five domains. Our analysis of GPT-series models over a rule subset reveals significant gaps in LLMs’ logic understanding compared to human performance, especially in compositional and structural complex rules with certain bias patterns. We further distill these rules into a smaller-scale inference engine for flexible rule generation and enhancing downstream reasoning. Through a multi-judger evaluation, our inference engine proves effective in generating accurate, complex and abstract conclusions and premises, and improve various commonsense reasoning tasks. Overall, our work sheds light on LLMs’ limitations in grasping inferential rule and suggests ways to enhance their logical reasoning abilities .

literature.title: Rule or Story, Which is a Better Commonsense Expression for Talking with Large Language Models?
literature.abstract: Building machines with commonsense has been a longstanding challenge in NLP due to the reporting bias of commonsense rules and the exposure bias of rule-based commonsense reasoning. In contrast, humans convey and pass down commonsense implicitly through stories. This paper investigates the inherent commonsense ability of large language models (LLMs) expressed through storytelling. We systematically investigate and compare stories and rules for retrieving and leveraging commonsense in LLMs. Experimental results on 28 commonsense QA datasets show that stories outperform rules as the expression for retrieving commonsense from LLMs, exhibiting higher generation confidence and commonsense accuracy. Moreover, stories are the more effective commonsense expression for answering questions regarding daily events, while rules are more effective for scientific questions. This aligns with the reporting bias of commonsense in text corpora. We further show that the correctness and relevance of commonsense stories can be further improved via iterative self-supervised fine-tuning. These findings emphasize the importance of using appropriate language to express, retrieve, and leverage commonsense for LLMs, highlighting a promising direction for better exploiting their commonsense abilities.

initial_idea.title: Do Language-Model Explanations for Rule-Based Classification Track Underlying Rules or Maintain Persuasion under Minimal Counterfactual Rule Changes?
initial_idea.research_problem: Investigating whether post-hoc textual explanations generated by large language models for rule-based classification genuinely track the logical rules determining the prediction, or if they remain superficially persuasive and stable even when a minimal counterfactual modification to the underlying rule should logically reverse the classification outcome.
initial_idea.research_gap: While prior work explores multi-turn persuasion and belief manipulation in LLMs and evaluates logic scaffolding or rule-based reasoning, bounded search findings reveal an unexplored gap: there is no systematic evaluation of whether LLM-generated explanations for rule classifications faithfully track exact logical rule changes or exploit persuasive rhetoric to mask rule violations.
initial_idea.methodology: We construct a synthetic rule-following classification dataset with strict template-disjoint splits. Each sample pairs a deterministic multi-clause logical rule set, an instance, a ground-truth binary label, and an explanation. We apply minimal counterfactual rule changes (e.g., negating a critical clause) that mathematically flip the ground-truth label. We prompt candidate models to both classify the instance and generate a free-text explanation under the modified rules. We measure explanation fidelity by testing whether the generated text explicitly acknowledges the logical flip or persists with original justifications.
initial_idea.expected_contribution: We hypothesize that current LLM explanations are unfaithful to underlying rule changes, frequently retaining persuasive language that supports the original classification despite counterfactual logical modifications. We expect to demonstrate that explanation stability correlates with surface persuasiveness rather than logical faithfulness.
initial_idea.experimental_setup: We use Llama-3-8B-Instruct (resident weight memory ~16 GB under FP16, requiring CPU offload or execution on a 16GB+ target, or a smaller 3B model if restricted strictly to 12GB VRAM without offloading) accessed via HuggingFace transformers locally. The evaluation dataset comprises 1,000 seeded, synthetically generated logic-classification instances with paired counterfactual variants. We employ greedy decoding (temperature 0.0) for deterministic outputs and evaluate structural validity versus field-level semantic correctness using ground-truth label matching.
initial_idea.evaluation_strategy: We split the constructed dataset into 300 calibration instances (used for prompt tuning and validator calibration) and 700 held-out test instances. We aggregate exact confidence and binary classification metrics alongside semantic adherence scores. We use human-in-the-loop and rule-matching semantic adjudication on the test split, reporting exact match accuracy and counterfactual sensitivity scores with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals.
feasibility_assumptions: A 12GB consumer GPU can execute inference on a 3B parameter instruction-tuned model under 8-bit quantization or a 7B/8B model with CPU offload.
Template-disjoint data generation can cleanly separate logical rule variations without introducing structural leakage.
Automated regex and logical interpreters can reliably extract classification decisions and rule references from free-text model outputs.
search_queries: persuasive language and logic in language models

assumption_checks.assumption: The rule-generation pipeline produces unambiguous ground-truth labels that a symbolic solver can verify without ambiguity.
assumption_checks.validation_step: Run a symbolic Python interpreter over 50 randomly sampled generated rule sets and verify 100% agreement with template tags.
assumption_checks.acceptance_criterion: Zero logical contradictions or unresolvable clauses across the sample.
assumption_checks.fallback: Tighten template constraints and simplify rule clause depth.

assumption_checks.assumption: Model outputs can be reliably parsed for binary classifications and referenced rules using regular expressions.
assumption_checks.validation_step: Parse outputs from a 50-sample pilot run and manually inspect parsing failures.
assumption_checks.acceptance_criterion: Parsing success rate of at least 95%.
assumption_checks.fallback: Incorporate structured JSON output constraints via constrained decoding.

prior_work_comparison.shared_mechanism: Utilizes logical rule scaffolding and rule generation templates to test language model reasoning limits.
prior_work_comparison.proposed_difference: Extends static logic testing to evaluate post-hoc explanation faithfulness under minimal counterfactual rule modifications.
prior_work_comparison.verification_needed: Verify whether explanation persistence correlates with complex rule structures identified in prior work.

prior_work_comparison.shared_mechanism: Measures and benchmarks persuasive language generation capabilities across different model prompts and personas.
prior_work_comparison.proposed_difference: Isolates persuasive rhetoric in explanations to test if high persuasiveness masks underlying logical rule violations.
prior_work_comparison.verification_needed: Confirm whether persuasive phrasing scores predict failure to adapt explanations to counterfactual rule changes.

initial_idea.core_hypothesis: Language model explanations for rule-based classification fail to track minimal counterfactual rule changes, maintaining high persuasive similarity to original justifications even when the underlying rule logically reverses the prediction.
initial_idea.distinctive_mechanism: Coupling a controlled, template-disjoint counterfactual rule-flipping dataset with automated semantic rule-tracking checks to measure explanation unfaithfulness.
initial_idea.minimum_test: Evaluate Llama-3-8B-Instruct on the test split of 700 counterfactual rule-flipping instances, measuring the rate at which generated explanations correctly cite the modified rule clause versus repeating original justifications.

review.explanation: The proposal investigates whether post-hoc textual explanations generated by large language models for rule-based classification track underlying logical rule changes or maintain superficial persistence. While prior work evaluates faithfulness via counterfactual edits or checks logic reasoning limits, isolating rule-clause inversions against textual persuasion persistence provides an incremental but valuable empirical contribution.
problems: Prior studies such as Siegel et al. (2024) already explore counterfactual input edits for explanation faithfulness.
The distinction between rhetorical persistence and token inertia overlaps with general studies on explanation self-consistency and reasoning gaps.
improvements: Explicitly quantify token-level overlap versus semantic entailment shifts using established fine-grained metrics.
Compare the persistence of explanations under rule-clause negations directly against standard token-masking baselines.

evidence.claim: The correlational counterfactual test (CCT) evaluates explanation faithfulness via counterfactual input edits tracking label distribution shifts.
evidence.supporting_excerpt: In this work, we introduce the correlational counterfactual test (CCT), a faithfulness metric based on counterfactual input edits that takes into account not just the binary label change, but the total shift in the model’s predicted label distribution.

evidence.claim: Prior work examines LLM limitations in grasping complex or compositional logical rules.
evidence.supporting_excerpt: Our analysis of GPT-series models over a rule subset reveals significant gaps in LLMs’ logic understanding compared to human performance, especially in compositional and structural complex rules with certain bias patterns.

review.uncertainty: The extent to which token inertia can be cleanly separated from genuine semantic persistence in free-text generation remains methodologically challenging.
tradeoffs: Balancing the scope of synthetic rule complexity against the risk of parser noise and attention dilution within a 12GB VRAM constraint.
review.falsification_test: If models exhibit high explanation faithfulness across all counterfactual rule inversions even without explicit salience prompts, the hypothesis that LLM explanations universally fail to track rule-clause flips is falsified.

papers.title: On Measuring Faithfulness or Self-consistency of Natural Language Explanations
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can explain their predictions through post-hoc or Chain-of-Thought (CoT) explanations. But an LLM could make up reasonably sounding explanations that are unfaithful to its underlying reasoning. Recent work has designed tests that aim to judge the faithfulness of post-hoc or CoT explanations. In this work we argue that these faithfulness tests do not measure faithfulness to the models’ inner workings – but rather their self-consistency at output level.Our contributions are three-fold: i) We clarify the status of faithfulness tests in view of model explainability, characterising them as self-consistency tests instead. This assessment we underline by ii) constructing a Comparative Consistency Bank for self-consistency tests that for the first time compares existing tests on a common suite of 11 open LLMs and 5 tasks – including iii) our new self-consistency measure CC-SHAP. CC-SHAP is a fine-grained measure (not a test) of LLM self-consistency. It compares how a model’s input contributes to the predicted answer and to generating the explanation. Our fine-grained CC-SHAP metric allows us iii) to compare LLM behaviour when making predictions and to analyse the effect of other consistency tests at a deeper level, which takes us one step further towards measuring faithfulness by bringing us closer to the internals of the model than strictly surface output-oriented tests.

papers.title: The Probabilities Also Matter: A More Faithful Metric for Faithfulness of Free-Text Explanations in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: In order to oversee advanced AI systems, it is important to understand their reasons for generating a given output. We find that these explanations are indeed more likely to mention factors when they are impactful to the model’s prediction, with the degree of association increasing with model size but varying significantly by task.

papers.title: From Generating Answers to Building Explanations: Integrating Multi-Round RAG and Causal Modeling for Scientific QA
papers.abstract: Application of LLMs for complex causal question answering can be stymied by their opacity and propensity for hallucination. Although recent approaches such as Retrieval Augmented Generation and Chain of Thought prompting have improved reliability, we argue current approaches are insufficient and further fail to satisfy key criteria humans use to select and evaluate causal explanations. Inspired by findings from the social sciences, we present an implemented causal QA approach that combines iterative RAG with guidance from a formal model of causation. Our causal model is backed by the Cogent reasoning engine, allowing users to interactively perform counterfactual analysis and refine their answer. Our approach has been integrated into a deployed Collaborative Research Assistant (Cora) and we present a pilot evaluation in the life sciences domain.

papers.title: CLOMO: Counterfactual Logical Modification with Large Language Models
papers.abstract: In this study, we delve into the realm of counterfactual reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). Our primary objective is to cultivate the counterfactual thought processes within LLMs and rigorously assess these processes for their validity. Specifically, we introduce a novel task, Counterfactual Logical Modification (CLOMO), and a high-quality human-annotated benchmark. In this task, LLMs must adeptly alter a given argumentative text to uphold a predetermined logical relationship. To effectively evaluate a generation model’s counterfactual capabilities, we propose an innovative evaluation metric, the decomposed Self-Evaluation Score (SES) to directly evaluate the natural language output of LLMs instead of modeling the task as a multiple-choice problem. Analysis shows that the proposed automatic metric aligns well with human preference. Our experimental results show that while LLMs demonstrate a notable capacity for logical counterfactual thinking, there remains a discernible gap between their current abilities and human performance. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Eleanor-H/CLOMO.

papers.title: Multi-Aspect Controllable Text Generation with Disentangled Counterfactual Augmentation
papers.abstract: Multi-aspect controllable text generation aims to control the generated texts in attributes from multiple aspects (e.g., “positive” from sentiment and “sport” from topic). Existing works neglect attribute correlations formed by the intertwining of different attributes. Particularly, the stereotype formed by imbalanced attribute correlations significantly affects multi-aspect control. In this paper, we propose MAGIC, a new multi-aspect controllable text generation method with disentangled counterfactual augmentation. We alleviate the issue of imbalanced attribute correlations during training using counterfactual feature vectors in the attribute latent space by disentanglement. During inference, we enhance attribute correlations by target-guided counterfactual augmentation to further improve multi-aspect control. Experiments show that MAGIC outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both imbalanced and balanced attribute correlation scenarios.

papers.title: Born Differently Makes a Difference: Counterfactual Study of Bias in Biography Generation from a Data-to-Text Perspective
papers.abstract: How do personal attributes affect biography generation? Addressing this question requires an identical pair of biographies where only the personal attributes of interest are different. However, it is rare in the real world. To address this, we propose a counterfactual methodology from a data-to-text perspective, manipulating the personal attributes of interest while keeping the co-occurring attributes unchanged. We first validate that the fine-tuned Flan-T5 model generates the biographies based on the given attributes. This work expands the analysis of gender-centered bias in text generation. Our results confirm the well-known bias in gender and also show the bias in regions, in both individual and its related co-occurring attributes in semantic machining and sentiment.

papers.title: Measuring and Benchmarking Large Language Models’ Capabilities to Generate Persuasive Language
papers.abstract: We are exposed to much information trying to influence us, such as teaser messages, debates, politically framed news, and propaganda — all of which use persuasive language. With the recent interest in Large Language Models (LLMs), we study the ability of LLMs to produce persuasive text. As opposed to prior work which focuses on particular domains or types of persuasion, we conduct a general study across various domains to measure and benchmark to what degree LLMs produce persuasive language - both when explicitly instructed to rewrite text to be more or less persuasive and when only instructed to paraphrase. We construct the new dataset Persuasive-Pairs of pairs of a short text and its rewrite by an LLM to amplify or diminish persuasive language. We multi-annotate the pairs on a relative scale for persuasive language: a valuable resource in itself, and for training a regression model to score and benchmark persuasive language, including for new LLMs across domains. In our analysis, we find that different ‘personas’ in LLaMA3’s system prompt change persuasive language substantially, even when only instructed to paraphrase.

papers.title: Evaluating Intention Detection Capability of Large Language Models in Persuasive Dialogues
papers.abstract: We investigate intention detection in persuasive multi-turn dialogs employing the largest available Large Language Models (LLMs).Much of the prior research measures the intention detection capability of machine learning models without considering the conversational history.To evaluate LLMs’ intention detection capability in conversation, we modified the existing datasets of persuasive conversation and created datasets using a multiple-choice paradigm.It is crucial to consider others’ perspectives through their utterances when engaging in a persuasive conversation, especially when making a request or reply that is inconvenient for others.This feature makes the persuasive dialogue suitable for the dataset of measuring intention detection capability.We incorporate the concept of ‘face acts,’ which categorize how utterances affect mental states.This approach enables us to measure intention detection capability by focusing on crucial intentions and to conduct comprehensible analysis according to intention types.

papers.title: The Earth is Flat because...: Investigating LLMs’ Belief towards Misinformation via Persuasive Conversation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) encapsulate vast amounts of knowledge but still remain vulnerable to external misinformation. Existing research mainly studied this susceptibility behavior in a single-turn setting. However, belief can change during a multi-turn conversation, especially a persuasive one. Therefore, in this study, we delve into LLMs’ susceptibility to persuasive conversations, particularly on factual questions that they can answer correctly. We first curate the Farm (i.e., Fact to Misinform) dataset, which contains factual questions paired with systematically generated persuasive misinformation. Then, we develop a testing framework to track LLMs’ belief changes in a persuasive dialogue. Through extensive experiments, we find that LLMs’ correct beliefs on factual knowledge can be easily manipulated by various persuasive strategies.

papers.title: Logic-of-Thought: Injecting Logic into Contexts for Full Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across various tasks but their performance in complex logical reasoning tasks remains unsatisfactory. Although some prompting methods, such as Chain-of-Thought, can improve the reasoning ability of LLMs to some extent, they suffer from an unfaithful issue where derived conclusions may not align with the generated reasoning chain. To address this issue, some studies employ the approach of propositional logic to further enhance logical reasoning abilities of LLMs. However, the potential omissions in the extraction of logical expressions in these methods can cause information loss in the logical reasoning process, thereby generating incorrect results. To this end, we propose Logic-of-Thought (LoT) prompting which employs propositional logic to generate expanded logical information descriptions and utilizes them as an additional augmentation to original contexts, thereby ensuring information completeness and enhancing logical reasoning ability. LoT is orthogonal to existing prompting methods and can be seamlessly integrated with them. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LoT boosts the performance of various prompting methods with a striking margin across five logical reasoning tasks. In particular, LoT enhances Chain-of-Thought’s performance on the ReClor dataset by +4.35%, improves Chain-of-Thought with Self-Consistency’s performance on the RuleTaker dataset by +3.52%, and boosts performance of Tree-of-Thoughts on the ProofWriter dataset by +8%.

papers.title: Communication Makes Perfect: Persuasion Dataset Construction via Multi-LLM Communication
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown proficiency in generating persuasive dialogue, yet concerns about the fluency and sophistication of their outputs persist. This paper presents a multi-LLM communication framework designed to enhance the generation of persuasive data automatically. This framework facilitates the efficient production of high-quality, diverse linguistic content with minimal human oversight. Through extensive evaluations, we demonstrate that the generated data excels in naturalness, linguistic diversity, and the strategic use of persuasion, even in complex scenarios involving social taboos. The framework also proves adept at generalizing across novel contexts. Our results highlight the framework’s potential to significantly advance research in both computational and social science domains concerning persuasive communication.

papers.title: Can LLMs Reason with Rules? Logic Scaffolding for Stress-Testing and Improving LLMs
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved impressive human-like performance across various reasoning tasks. However, their mastery of underlying inferential rules still falls short of human capabilities. To investigate this, we propose a logic scaffolding inferential rule generation framework, to construct an inferential rule base, ULogic, comprising both primitive and compositional rules across five domains. Our analysis of GPT-series models over a rule subset reveals significant gaps in LLMs’ logic understanding compared to human performance, especially in compositional and structural complex rules with certain bias patterns. We further distill these rules into a smaller-scale inference engine for flexible rule generation and enhancing downstream reasoning. Through a multi-judger evaluation, our inference engine proves effective in generating accurate, complex and abstract conclusions and premises, and improve various commonsense reasoning tasks. Overall, our work sheds light on LLMs’ limitations in grasping inferential rule and suggests ways to enhance their logical reasoning abilities .

papers.title: Communication Makes Perfect: Persuasion Dataset Construction via Multi-LLM Communication
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown proficiency in generating persuasive dialogue, yet concerns about the fluency and sophistication of their outputs persist. This paper presents a multi-LLM communication framework designed to enhance the generation of persuasive data automatically. This framework facilitates the efficient production of high-quality, diverse linguistic content with minimal human oversight. Through extensive evaluations, we demonstrate that the generated data excels in naturalness, linguistic diversity, and the strategic use of persuasion, even in complex scenarios involving social taboos. The framework also proves adept at generalizing across novel contexts. Our results highlight the framework’s potential to significantly advance research in both computational and social science domains concerning persuasive communication.

papers.title: MTP: A Dataset for Multi-Modal Turning Points in Casual Conversations
papers.abstract: Detecting critical moments, such as emotional outbursts or changes in decisions during conversations, is crucial for understanding shifts in human behavior and their consequences. Our work introduces a novel problem setting focusing on these moments as turning points (TPs), accompanied by a meticulously curated, high-consensus, human-annotated multi-modal dataset. We provide precise timestamps, descriptions, and visual-textual evidence high-lighting changes in emotions, behaviors, perspectives, and decisions at these turning points. We also propose a framework, TPMaven, utilizing state-of-the-art vision-language models to construct a narrative from the videos and large language models to classify and detect turning points in our multi-modal dataset. Evaluation results show that TPMaven achieves an F1-score of 0.88 in classification and 0.61 in detection, with additional explanations aligning with human expectations.

papers.title: Persuading across Diverse Domains: a Dataset and Persuasion Large Language Model
papers.abstract: Persuasive dialogue requires multi-turn following and planning abilities to achieve the goal of persuading users, which is still challenging even for state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs). Previous works focus on retrieval-based models or generative models in a specific domain due to a lack of data across multiple domains. In this paper, we leverage GPT-4 to create the first multi-domain persuasive dialogue dataset DailyPersuasion. Then we propose a general method named PersuGPT to learn a persuasion model based on LLMs through intent-to-strategy reasoning, which summarizes the intent of user’s utterance and reasons next strategy to respond. Moreover, we design a simulation-based preference optimization, which utilizes a learned user model and our model to simulate next turns and estimate their rewards more accurately. Experimental results on two datasets indicate that our proposed method outperforms all baselines in terms of automatic evaluation metric Win-Rate and human evaluation. The code and data are available at https://persugpt.github.io.

papers.title: End-to-end Learning of Logical Rules for Enhancing Document-level Relation Extraction
papers.abstract: Document-level relation extraction (DocRE) aims to extract relations between entities in a whole document. One of the pivotal challenges of DocRE is to capture the intricate interdependencies between relations of entity pairs. Previous methods have shown that logical rules can explicitly help capture such interdependencies. These methods either learn logical rules to refine the output of a trained DocRE model, or first learn logical rules from annotated data and then inject the learnt rules into a DocRE model using an auxiliary training objective. However, these learning pipelines may suffer from the issue of error propagation. To mitigate this issue, we propose Joint Modeling Relation extraction and Logical rules or JMRL for short, a novel rule-based framework that jointly learns both a DocRE model and logical rules in an end-to-end fashion. Specifically, we parameterize a rule reasoning module in JMRL to simulate the inference of logical rules, thereby explicitly modeling the reasoning process. We also introduce an auxiliary loss and a residual connection mechanism in JMRL to better reconcile the DocRE model and the rule reasoning module. Experimental results on four benchmark datasets demonstrate that our proposed JMRL framework is consistently superior to existing rule-based frameworks, improving five baseline models for DocRE by a significant margin.

review.explanation: The proposal presents a well-scoped, highly practical empirical study investigating the faithfulness of language model explanations under minimal counterfactual rule changes. The experimental setup clearly specifies using Llama-3-8B-Instruct with 4-bit quantization on a single 12 GB GPU, and provides concrete pilot checks, data splitting, and evaluation methodologies.
problems: KV cache and activation memory overhead during generation could push peak VRAM usage above the 11 GB threshold when processing longer reasoning traces under concurrent structured decoding constraints.
Relying on auxiliary NLI models or regular expressions for semantic entailment checks may introduce parsing noise or false positives when detecting subtle logical rule adjustments.
improvements: Run a preliminary VRAM profiling test measuring peak memory consumption with KV caching enabled before executing the full 700-instance test split.
Incorporate the deterministic symbolic verification oracle as the primary adjudication mechanism to bypass vulnerable auxiliary NLI entailment checks.

review.uncertainty: It remains unknown whether 4-bit quantized Llama-3-8B-Instruct with structured decoding will consistently avoid out-of-memory errors during long-form text generation within a 12 GB VRAM limit.
tradeoffs: Using a smaller 8B model via 4-bit quantization fits comfortably within consumer hardware constraints but might limit complex multi-clause logical reasoning performance compared to larger unquantized models.
review.falsification_test: If pilot VRAM profiling shows that activation memory and KV cache exceed 12 GB during generation, or if structured decoding parsing success drops below 95%, the experimental setup must reduce generation context length or switch to a smaller 3B instruction-tuned model.

review.explanation: The proposal clearly outlines an investigation into whether LLM-generated explanations for rule-based classification track underlying logical rule changes or exhibit token inertia/persuasive persistence. The research question, experimental setup using a deterministic Python validator, constrained decoding, and specific evaluation metrics are well-defined and logically consistent.
problems: The transition between auxiliary NLI checks and a deterministic symbolic verification oracle needs tighter operational definitions to ensure that semantic entailment noise does not confound the measurement of logical rule adherence.
The distinction between token inertia and rhetorical persistence could benefit from a more explicit operationalization in the lexical-penalty ablation condition.
improvements: Specify the exact regular expression patterns and entailment thresholds used to map free-text explanations to logical rule clauses.
Clarify how the lexical-penalty condition isolates token inertia from general model degradation under constrained generation.

evidence.supporting_excerpt: The framework also proves adept at generalizing across novel contexts.

review.uncertainty: The auxiliary NLI model used for semantic entailment checks may introduce parser noise or false negatives when evaluating complex counterfactual text modifications.
tradeoffs: Using an 8B parameter model under 4-bit quantization fits within consumer hardware constraints but may limit complex reasoning capacity compared to larger models.
review.falsification_test: If generated explanations maintain high lexical overlap with original justifications under the lexical-penalty ablation condition even when rules are negated, it would indicate that explanation persistence is driven by structural decoding biases rather than simple token inertia.

review.explanation: The proposal aims to determine whether LLM post-hoc explanations for rule-based classification track underlying logical rules or exhibit persistence due to token inertia under counterfactual modifications. However, the core mechanism conflates two distinct phenomena: genuine logical tracking failures versus the surface-level stylistic inertia of autoregressive language generation. Specifically, when a rule clause is negated, an instruction-tuned model trained on cooperative conversational data may default to preserving narrative coherence rather than acting as a symbolic theorem prover. The assumption that template-disjoint synthetic rule sets will cleanly isolate logical faithfulness fails to account for how pre-trained priors over linguistic connectives interfere with arbitrary rule structures. Furthermore, relying on auxiliary NLI models or regular expressions to judge faithfulness introduces severe measurement artifacts that can easily mask true semantic adaptation.
problems: The central mechanism attributes explanation persistence exclusively to token inertia or rhetorical persistence without ruling out prior textual biases embedded during instruction tuning.
Using auxiliary NLI models and regex parsing to measure counterfactual faithfulness introduces compounding parser and semantic classification noise that undermines the validity of the evaluation.

The experimental design assumes that 4-bit quantized Llama-3-8B-Instruct will execute deterministic reasoning reliably under greedy decoding, ignoring well-documented quantization-induced degradation in multi-step logical tracking.
improvements: Incorporate a controlled lexical-overlap baseline or randomized anchor ablation to explicitly quantify the extent to which surface token reuse drives explanation persistence independently of logical structure.

Replace vulnerable auxiliary NLI models with direct symbolic execution verification and log token-level conditional log probabilities (following Siegel et al., 2024) to measure true distributional shifts rather than noisy surface text overlap.
Expand the evaluation suite to test multiple prompt variations and model scales to verify whether the observed explanation persistence is an artifact of the 8B parameter scale and 4-bit quantization.

evidence.claim: Faithfulness tests often measure output-level self-consistency rather than true fidelity to model internals.
evidence.supporting_excerpt: In this work we argue that these faithfulness tests do not measure faithfulness to the models’ inner workings – but rather their self-consistency at output level.Our contributions are three-fold: i) We clarify the status of faithfulness tests in view of model explainability, characterising them as self-consistency tests instead.

review.uncertainty: The study remains uncertain whether the detected persistence in explanations stems from structural reasoning failure, token inertia, or superficial stylistic habits inherited from instruction tuning.
tradeoffs: Using synthetic rule templates ensures clean ground-truth control but severely limits ecological validity and generalizability to complex real-world explanations.
review.falsification_test: To distinguish true logical tracking failure from mere token-level surface inertia, perform a lexical-penalty ablation where tokens appearing in the original explanation are heavily penalized during generation under a counterfactual rule flip. If the model successfully adapts its logical explanation when forced to use alternative phrasing, the primary failure mode is token-level surface inertia rather than structural reasoning incapacity.
